A_target.statement:
Let $p$ and $q$ be [[Definition:Prime Number|primes]] with $q \divides 2^p - 1$.
Then:
:$q \equiv 1 \pmod p$

B_source.statement:
Let $G$ be a [[Definition:Finite Group|finite group]] and $g \in G$.
Then the [[Definition:Order of Group Element|order]] of $g$ divides $\order G$.

object_map.reformulation: Specialize Lagrange's theorem to the class of 2 modulo q, whose order is forced to be p.

validity_conditions: q is odd as 2^p - 1 is odd, so 2 is invertible modulo q.
p must be prime, so that the order of 2, which divides p and is not 1, equals p.
proof_plan: $2^p - 1$ is odd, so $q$ is odd and the class of $2$ lies in $\paren {\Z / q \Z}^\times$, a group of order $q - 1$.

As $2^p \equiv 1 \pmod q$, the order of $2$ divides $p$.
It is not $1$, as $2 \not \equiv 1 \pmod q$, so it equals $p$.

Hence every prime divisor of the [[Definition:Mersenne Number|Mersenne number]] $2^p - 1$ satisfies $q \equiv 1 \pmod p$.
{{qed}}
